modules.title: HTML & CSS Fundamentals
modules.description: Learn the building blocks of web pages

lessons.title: HTML Document Structure
lessons.description: Understand the anatomy of an HTML document

steps.content: Every HTML document follows a standard structure. The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration tells the browser this is HTML5. The <html> element wraps everything, with <head> containing metadata (title, charset, viewport) and <body> containing visible content.

The <head> section includes: <meta charset="UTF-8"> for character encoding, <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> for responsive design, and <title> for the browser tab text. These don't appear on the page but are crucial for proper rendering.

steps.question: What does the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration do?
options: Declares this is an HTML5 document
steps.explanation: <!DOCTYPE html> is not an HTML tag; it's a declaration that tells the browser to render the page in standards mode for HTML5.
hints: It's the very first line in an HTML file
It doesn't have a closing tag

steps.question: The element that contains metadata like title and charset is <______>.
steps.explanation: The <head> element contains document metadata - information about the page that isn't displayed directly.

steps.question: Order these tags to create a valid HTML5 document structure
steps.explanation: DOCTYPE first, then html wrapper, then head with metadata, then body with visible content.

steps.question: The <title> element appears in the browser tab, not on the page itself.
steps.explanation: The <title> goes in <head> and shows in the browser tab, bookmarks, and search results - not in the page content area.
hints: Check where <title> is placed in the document structure

lessons.title: Semantic HTML Elements
lessons.description: Use meaningful tags for better accessibility and SEO

steps.content: Semantic HTML uses elements that describe their meaning: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <footer>. These help screen readers, search engines, and developers understand page structure without reading CSS classes.

Before semantic elements, developers used <div class="header"> or <div id="nav">. Semantic tags replace these with meaningful names. For example, <nav> clearly indicates navigation links, while <main> identifies the primary content area (only one per page).

steps.question: Which element should wrap the main navigation links?
steps.explanation: <nav> is specifically designed for navigation sections. While often placed inside <header>, the <nav> element itself semantically marks navigation links.
hints: It's not <header> - that's for the page header area

steps.question: How many <main> elements should a page have?
steps.explanation: HTML spec allows exactly one <main> element per document. It represents the dominant content of the <body>.
hints: The spec is strict about this

steps.question: An independent, self-contained piece of content (like a blog post) uses the <______> element.
steps.explanation: <article> represents a complete, self-contained composition that could be syndicated (e.g., blog post, news article, forum post).
hints: It's distinct from <section> which groups related content

steps.question: Order these semantic elements in a typical page layout
steps.explanation: Header (with nav) at top, main content in middle, footer at bottom.
hints: Top to bottom: header, main, footer

steps.question: A <section> element must always have a heading (h1-h6) as a child.
steps.explanation: The HTML spec recommends that each <section> have a heading to identify its topic. This improves accessibility and document outline.
hints: Headings label what the section is about

lessons.title: CSS Box Model
lessons.description: Understand how elements are sized and spaced

steps.content: Every HTML element is a rectangular box with four layers: content (text/images), padding (space around content), border (edge around padding), and margin (space outside border). The total width = content width + padding + border + margin.

By default, width/height apply to the content box only. Adding padding or border increases the total element size. The box-sizing: border-box property changes this so width/height include padding and border, making layouts much more predictable.

steps.question: What is the default value of box-sizing?
steps.explanation: The default is content-box, meaning width/height only include the content area. Padding and border add to the total size.
hints: This is why layouts often break unexpectedly

steps.question: The space between an element's border and the next element is called ______.
steps.explanation: Margin creates space outside the border. It's transparent and doesn't have a background color. Margins can collapse vertically.
hints: It's the outermost layer of the box model

steps.question: Order these CSS declarations from innermost to outermost layer
steps.explanation: The box model layers from inside out: content → padding → border → margin.

steps.question: Vertical margins between adjacent elements collapse into the larger margin.
steps.explanation: Margin collapse means if one element has margin-bottom: 20px and the next has margin-top: 30px, the space between them is 30px (the larger), not 50px.
hints: This only happens with vertical margins

steps.question: If an element has width: 200px, padding: 20px, border: 5px, and box-sizing: content-box, what is its total rendered width?
steps.explanation: With content-box: total = 200 (content) + 40 (padding left+right) + 10 (border left+right) = 250px.
hints: Remember padding and border are on both sides
box-sizing: content-box means width is content only

lessons.title: Flexbox Layout
lessons.description: Create flexible, responsive layouts with Flexbox

steps.content: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for arranging items in rows or columns. Apply display: flex to a container to make its children flex items. The container controls alignment, distribution, and ordering of items.

Key container properties: flex-direction (row, column), justify-content (main axis alignment), align-items (cross axis alignment), gap (spacing), flex-wrap (wrapping). Key item properties: flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, align-self.

steps.question: What is the default flex-direction?
steps.explanation: The default flex-direction is row, which arranges items left-to-right horizontally. The main axis is horizontal, cross axis is vertical.
hints: Think of reading direction in English

steps.question: The property that aligns items on the main axis is ______.
steps.explanation: justify-content controls main axis alignment: flex-start, flex-end, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly.
hints: It's about 'justifying' content along the main axis

steps.question: Order these to create a centered card using Flexbox
steps.explanation: Container → flex → center main axis → center cross axis → full viewport height = perfectly centered.
hints: Need both justify-content and align-items for perfect centering

steps.question: The gap property works on both flex and grid containers.
steps.explanation: gap (and row-gap/column-gap) is now supported in both Flexbox and Grid layouts, providing consistent spacing between items.
hints: It used to be grid-gap only

steps.question: To make a flex item take up remaining space, you set:
steps.explanation: flex-grow: 1 tells the item to expand and fill available space on the main axis. Multiple items with flex-grow share space proportionally.

steps.question: To allow flex items to wrap to the next line, set flex-wrap: ______.
steps.explanation: By default flex-wrap is nowrap (all items on one line). Setting wrap allows items to flow to new lines when they don't fit.
